full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff opposite party brought the suit for partition of her 8 annas share in the suit land comprised of 4 plots with an additional prayer for purchasing the 8 annas shaft of the defendant-in the dwellings house in plot No. 492 under section 4 of the Partition Act. 

 3. The plaintiffs case was that the suit land belonged to Amritolal on whose death it devolved upon his two sons Jadab and Madusudan each having 8 annas share. Upon death of Jadab his 8 annas share deloved upon the plaintiff alone as his daughter and the 8 annas share of Modusudan devolved upon his only son and heir Jogobandhu. Plaintiff and his paternal cousin Jogobandhu jointly possessed the suit land including the dwelling house situated on plot No. 492. Jogobandhu transferred his entire share to the defendant in 1956 and 1957. Defendant being stranger and also having belonged to different that is muslim community the plaintiff is entitled to buy up the defendant's share in the dwelling house and joint possession being also inconvenient the plaintiff is entitled to have partition of her share of the other land. The demand for partition purchase having not been met this suit was brought. 

 4. The defence case was that there was already a partition between plaintiff and Jogobandhu and that Jogobandhu and after him his vendees namely the defendants have been separately possessing their share of lands. So there is no cause of partition. It was also pleaded that the plaintiff, since after her marriage having lived away with her husband she was no longer a member of her paternal family and she also did not possessed the dwelling house and as such she could not claim to purchase the defendants share of dwelling house under section 4 of the Partition Act. Further it was pleaded that no partition suit having been brought by the defendants the claim under section 4 of the Partition Act not lie. 

 The learned Munsif upon consideration of the evidence held that the defendants failed to show any previous partition and that the witnesses four the pin tiff and the defendants consistently proved that both the plaintiff and the defendants' vendor Jogobandhu used to live in the dwelling house and that the suit properties being undivided joint properties of both the plaintiffs and Jogobandhu the vendor of the defendants and Jogobandhu having transferred his share of the dwelling house to defendants who were strangers and belong to a different community so the plaintiff was entitled to have partition of her share of the suit lands and also entitled to purchase the defendants' share in the dwelling house and the homestead land on plot No. 492. With the aforesaid finding he decreed the suit and directed assessment to the value of the dwelling house by a pleader Commissioner. 

 6. The defendants preferred appeal Before the appellate court the defendants raised 3 points of objection against the decree namely that the plaintiff ceased to be member of the undivided family after her marriage elsewhere and that the suit was not brought by the defendants namely the stranger purchaser, and therefore the plaintiffs' claim under section 4 of partition Act could not be legally maintained. The third point of objection was that the learned Munsif did not himself assessed the value of the property as was required by law. 

 7. The learned Subordinate Judge upon a consideration of all the evidence and the judgment of the trial court in the light of the objections made by the defendants found that since the plaintiff not only owns the family dwelling house but also resides there so she being a member of the family had locus standi to claim purchase of the share of stranger defendants under section 4 of the Partition Act. He also held that the suit even though it was filed by the plaintiff herself and not by the defendant stranger she was entitled to lay her claim under section 4 of the partition Act. Lastly he held that the learned Munsif did not commit any illegality in assessing the value of the purchased share through a pleader Commissioner. The learned Subordinate Judge also referred to certain decision of the superior court in support of his finding. Thus he rejected all the points of objection raised by the defend ants and by concurring with the findings of learned Munsif he affirmed the judgment and decree that was passed by the learned Munsif. 

 Firstly it was submitted that the courts below did not properly cons per the defendants' plea that there was a previous partition between the plaintiff and defendants, vendor Jogobaddhu after which the plaintiff did not continue to be a co-sharer in the suit land and was not entitled to claim partition it was also submitted that the courts below also failed to consider that the plaintiff since after her marriage lived away with her husband and thus ceased to be member of his paternal family. In this respect it appears from the judgments of the courts below that the learned Munsif after considering the evidence clearly found that there was no proof of any previous partition between the plaintiff and the defendants' vendor Jogobandhu or with the defendants. It was also observed by the learned Munsif that the defendants themselves conceded to a decree for partition except only the claim for purchase under section 4 of the Partition Act. The judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge shows that defendants did not raise any please of previous partition. 

 Mr. Anser Ali by referring to section 4 of the Partition Act submitted that the plaintiff could not be regarded as a member of the undivided family of her father after her marriage. 

 On the other hand Mr. B.N Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party contended that in order to be entitled to make a claim under section 4 of the Partition Act all that was necessary was that the plaintiff should own the house by having not divided the dwelling house with the members of her family in order to have her claim under section 4 of the partition suit. 

 10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury referred to several decision in support of his contention. In the case of Khtrode Chandra Goshal Vs. Saroda Proshid Mitra reported in XII CLJ page 525 it has been held that "undivided family" must be taken to mean, "undivided qua the dwelling house in question and to be a family which owns the house but has not divided it". The said decision has been followed in the case of Boto Krishna Vs. Akhoy Kumar reported in 115 C.W.N, page 450. In this case both the courts below have concurrently found that there was no previous partition between the plaintiffs and her paternal cousin and that both of them continue to live jointly in their paternal dwelling house. So upon the aforesaid facts the plaintiff has been rightly found to be entitled to lay her claim under section 4 of the Partition Act. So the points raised by Mr. Anser Ali in this regard does not stand. 

 11. Mr. Anser Ali next submitted that according to section 4 of the Partition Act only when the stranger transferee sues for partition then only the claim under that section can be laid. But in this case as the stranger transferees namely the defendants did not bring the suit for partition and the suit was brought by the plaintiff herself so section 4 was not applicable. Mr. Anser Ali is contention is apparently consistent with the wordings of the section. But this contention no longer holds in view of several decisions which have been cited by Mr. B.N Chowdhury In the case of Md. Magdu Bhuiva Vs. Jobhan Huq reported in 11 DLR page 355 it has been held that section 4 of the Partition Act will also apply in a case instituted by any other co-sharer because in a suit for partition all the parties are in the capacity of the plaintiff. In the case of Aid Habihullah Vs. Movi. Salek reported in 20 DLR page 489 the same principle has been followed. Besides that there were several other decision accepting the same proposition of law. So this points of objection raised by Mr. Anser Ali does not also stand. 

 12. Thirdly, Mr Anser Ali submitted that since the defendants being stranger and members of different community have admittedly purchased 1/2 share of the dwelling house in as early as in 1956 and 1957 and have been continuously possessing the same house along with the plaintiff and since the plaintiff did not lay any claim under section 4 of the Partition Act during the long past 19 years the present claim is unreasonable and should not be accepted In reply to this objection Mr. B.N. Chowdhury submitted that for bringing a suit for partition or for making the claim under section 4 of the partition act law has not enjoined any time limit and as such the plaintiff has a legal right to avail of the benefit of section 4 no matter that there has been delay in laying such claim. It is undisputed position of law that there is no time limit for laying a claim under section 4 of the Partition Act unlike the claim for preemption under other law. So the plaintiff having the benefit provided by the law itself there is no scope for this court to refuse the claim of the plaintiff on the ground that the claim has been laid after much delay. So I am unable to accept the contention of Mr. Anser Ali. Mr. Anser Ali raised another objection on the ground that by the decree, the learned Munsif did not assess the value of the purchased share of the dwelling house and left the assessment with the pleader Commissioner and this was illegal. Section 4 of the Partition Act requires that the courts shall make valuation in such manner as it thinks fit. This means that the manner of the assessment of value has been left by the law to the discretion of the court. In this case if the court directed assessment of value by physical verification by the commissioner that did not mean that the final assessment would not he made by the court after considering the report of the Commissioner This aspect has been duly considered by the learned Subordinate Judge and I accept the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge that there has been no illegality on that count. 

 13. Lastly, Mr. Anser Ali submitted that the courts below granted decree allowing plaintiff opposite party to purchase under section 4 of the Partition Act the defendant-petitioners' share of the entire homestead land and building appertaining to plot No. 492 which totally measures 3.71 lands while dwelling but covered only 15 lands of the plots. But according to section 4 of the Partition Act plaintiff was entitled to purchase the defendants' share only of the dwelling house and not the entire land of plot No. 492. So the decree in that regard was illegal having been passed in excess of the jurisdiction of the court. Mr. B N. Chowdhury submitted that the entire plot being the homestead plot containing the dwelling house plaintiff was entitled to purchased the defendants, share of the entire homestead plot and the decree did not suffer from any illegality nor lack of Jurisdiction in passing the decree. 

 14. On looking into the plaint as it is stood upon amendment by an application made by the plaintiff to insert the claim for purchase under section 4 of the Partition Act it clearly appears that plaintiff O.P, prayed for allowing her to purchase the defendants' share only in the dwelling house that stood on Plot No. 492. But the decree passed by the learned Mnnsif and affirmed by the learned Sub-Judge was in the following language: 

 This certainly means that the decree al-lowed the plaintiff to purchase not only the dwelling house but also homestead land of plot No. 492 without specifying the extent of the homestead land and thereby indicating that plaintiff's purchase was allowed for the entire plot No. 492 which totally measure 3.71. Neither in the plaint nor in the evidence there was any disclosure from the side of the plaintiff as to how much land of plot 492 was actually covered by the dwelling house and the courts below neither noticed this nor sought to ascertain this. Mr. B N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party submitted that the dwelling house as contained in section 4 of the partition Act will mean not only the structure of the house but also the attached land, garden etc. which are required for convenience use of the dwelling house. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury referred to certain decision for giving the meaning of the term dwelling house. In the case reported in 12 CLJ page 525 is have been held that the dwelling house embraces not merely the structure or building but includes also adjacent building, cartilage, garden Courtyard, orchard all that is necessary for the convenient occupation of their house. It must be reasonably held that the dwelling house as mentioning under section 4 of the partition act must indicate not only the structure of the house but also the adjunct land including courtyard which are essentially, necessary for reasonably convenient use of the dwelling house. In this case as I have already mentioned the plot No. 492 upon which the dwelling hat stands measure 3.71 i.e. over 1 Bighas lands. It cannot be conceived that the referred dwelling house of the plaintiff will cover the entire huge plot. So the plaintiff opposite party, under section 4 of the Partition Act will be entitled to purchase the share of the defendant-purchasers only so much land of the plot which is covered by the dwelling house and the adjunct land which are reasonably necessary for convenient and proper use of the house. Neither the plaintiff mentions the area of the dwelling house that is the actual quantum of land covered by the dwelling house and its adjunct land nor the courts ascertained or specified the same but gave a decree in favour of the plaintiff allowing her to purchase the entire homestead land that is the entire 3.71 land of plot No. 492. This was illegal being contrary to the provision of law and was also without jurisdiction. So on this ground alone the judgment and decree passed by the courts below can not be sustained and are liable to be set aside.
